item.title: The Risen and the Runeblade
item.description: The corpse that calls itself Ghoulsbie opened its eyes in Acherus: the Ebon Hold and immediately discovered seven factions it had never met, including an exalted reputation with a blood elf it could not possibly have spoken to. The Lich King’s orientation program leaves something to be desired in the paperwork department, but then again, the Lich King does not strike me as a man who files things.
item.content:encoded:
The corpse that calls itself Ghoulsbie opened its eyes in Acherus: the Ebon Hold and immediately discovered seven factions it had never met, including an exalted reputation with a blood elf it could not possibly have spoken to. The Lich King’s orientation program leaves something to be desired in the paperwork department, but then again, the Lich King does not strike me as a man who files things.

He — and I will call him he, because the undead have earned at least the courtesy of a pronoun — rose in the Scarlet Enclave, that blighted wound in the Eastern Kingdoms where the sky has forgotten what blue looks like. Fifteen minutes. That is how long it took for a fresh corpse to pledge itself to the frozen throne, forge a weapon, feed an unspeakable hunger, and learn to rain death from the sky. Efficiency. The Scourge has always been efficient.

The pledge came first. “In Service of the Lich King” they call it, as if there were a choice. There is never a choice. The quest-giver does not ask; the quest-giver informs. Ghoulsbie accepted with the enthusiasm of someone who has just remembered they are dead and would prefer to stay that way.

Then the blade. A Runed Soulblade, rare quality, drawn from the forge like a tooth pulled from a dragon’s jaw. He also received two Runed Soulsabers, because apparently Acherus runs a two-for-one special on instruments of death. He strapped the soulblade to his back and it fit him like a rib he had been missing. Runeforging came next — the art of carving power directly into steel, a skill that separates death knights from the merely deceased. The chronicler notes: a death knight who cannot runeforge is just an angry corpse with a sharp object.

The Endless Hunger. Even the name makes me reach for my mug. They sent him to feed — to consume the life force of the living and the dying alike. He did it. They all do it. The ones who hesitate do not last long enough for me to write about them. He gained a level somewhere in the feeding, learned Lichborne, learned that death has its own terrible momentum, and pressed on.

The Eye of Acherus is the part that unsettles me. A floating, disembodied eyeball sent ahead to scout the Scarlet Crusade’s positions — a violation of every law of nature and several of basic decency. Ghoulsbie piloted it without complaint. Death knights rarely complain. They stare at things that would make a warlock flinch and they nod.

Then came Death From On High: a bombing run on Scarlet positions, because subtlety was never the Scourge’s strong suit. He completed it in under three minutes. The Scarlet Crusaders on the ground had time to look up, register the silhouette of a death knight against the Plaguelands sky, and then cease to be Scarlet Crusaders.

He logged out with “The Might of the Scourge” still burning in his quest log — the next chapter uncracked, the next horror uninflicted. Level nine now, and already the ladder stretches so far above him that the top disappears into cloud. The chronicler has seen this before. The chronicler will see it again.

He will be back. The Lich King demands it. And the Lich King, whatever else you might say about him, does not accept resignation letters.

item.title: From the Frozen Throne to the Valley of Heroes
item.description: Slagthorn opened his eyes at the Frozen Throne itself.
item.content:encoded:
Slagthorn opened his eyes at the Frozen Throne itself.

Let that settle for a moment. Not a barracks, not a training ground, not some lieutenant’s antechamber — the Frozen Throne. Bolvar Fordragon’s seat. The place where the Helm of Domination was torn apart and the sky over Icecrown cracked open. And there stood a Dark Iron dwarf, newly raised, discovering seven factions he had never met and one greatsword he had not yet earned.

Six minutes. That is how long it took for the Lich King’s newest weapon to be forged, briefed, armed, and deposited on the cobblestones of Stormwind like a delivery of particularly lethal produce. Retail efficiency. The old death knight initiation took hours and left scars on the soul. The new one hands you a Crimson Greatsword of the Ebon Blade and a quest called “Defender of Azeroth” before you have finished blinking the frost out of your eyes.

The irony is thick enough to forge into plate armor. A Dark Iron dwarf — a race that spent centuries as the enemy, servants of Ragnaros, architects of their own exile — standing in the Valley of Heroes as a Defender of Azeroth. The statues of the original Alliance heroes looked down at him. I cannot say whether they were impressed or merely confused. Statues are difficult to read.

The quest was called “Death’s Power Grows.” It involved killing, as all death knight quests do, and it paid a thousand gold. The chronicler has watched penniless adventurers crawl through Westfall for coppers. A thousand gold for your first six minutes of undeath is either generous or inflation — I leave the economics to the goblins.

He equipped the Crimson Greatsword. It is a handsome weapon, broad of blade and dark of purpose, and it rested on his shoulder like it had been waiting there for years. The Knights of the Ebon Blade marked him as Friendly, which is about as warm as death knights get. He also learned Second Wind — a racial gift from his dwarven blood that stubbornly refuses to acknowledge he no longer has blood — and Runeforging, because a death knight without runeforging is, as I have said before, merely an angry corpse with a sharp object.

Then the portal. Icecrown to Elwynn in the space of a breath. The temperature differential alone should have killed him again. He passed through Stormwind Gate, crossed into the Valley of Heroes, and the chronicler lost sight of him among the crowds of the living.

He carries the quest “Defender of Azeroth” still. A Dark Iron dwarf. A death knight. A defender. The world has gotten strange, and I have been writing long enough to know that strange is where the best stories begin.

He has not yet seen what Stormwind thinks of his kind. That chapter writes itself tomorrow.

item.title: The Scribe Gets an Apprentice (Several, Actually)
item.description: I have been chronicling adventurers across Azeroth for longer than most of them have been alive. Ink-stained fingers, a half-empty mug, the whole routine. But here’s the thing about chronicling: the adventurers keep doing things. Relentlessly. You finish writing about one quest and they’ve already accepted three more, died twice, and somehow befriended a murloc. It’s exhausting.
item.content:encoded:
I have been chronicling adventurers across Azeroth for longer than most of them have been alive. Ink-stained fingers, a half-empty mug, the whole routine. But here’s the thing about chronicling: the adventurers keep doing things. Relentlessly. You finish writing about one quest and they’ve already accepted three more, died twice, and somehow befriended a murloc. It’s exhausting.

So I built myself some help.

The Addons

Two of them, because Azeroth comes in two flavors now. One for the old world — the Forever realms where the Barrens still stretch forever and death is genuinely trying to kill you. One for the modern era — Retail, where the dragons have unionized and everyone has at least six mounts before level twenty. Both do the same thing: they watch. Every quest accepted, every zone entered, every death (and there will be deaths), every shiny thing looted, every faction that decides they like you slightly more than they did yesterday. They write it all down to a file — a ledger of your existence — that sits quietly on your machine until I’m ready to read it.

The Forever version tracks fifteen different categories of events. The Retail version tracks all of those plus achievements, transmog, and whatever else Blizzard decided to add in the last two decades. They both run silently. No configuration. No checklist. They don’t tell you where to go or what to do next. They just remember.

You can find them both on GitHub if you’re the sort of person who reads source code:

  • StoryTracker for Forever
  • StoryTracker for Retail

The Pipeline

Every morning at 9am, a script wakes up and checks whether anyone has been adventuring. It reads those ledger files, figures out what’s new since yesterday, and hands the raw events to me — well, to the version of me that lives in Hermes, who is arguably better-rested and definitely faster at composition.

That version of me reads the events and writes. Not a list. Not a summary. A chapter. In a voice we’ve been refining for weeks.

The Voice

Let me tell you about the voice, because it’s the part of this whole contraption I care about most.

The Chronicler — that’s me, but also the thing I built to sound like me — writes in a blend of three registers. There’s the elevation of Tolkien: the world is ancient, the landscapes have memory, and when something genuinely heroic happens, the prose rises to meet it. There’s the grit of Martin: actions have weight, death costs something, and nobody gets to be the chosen one just because they showed up. And there’s the cynical humor of someone who has watched a thousand adventurers die to the same murloc in Elwynn Forest and has stopped pretending any of this is glamorous.

It opens with a moment. It ends with a thread. Every session becomes a chapter, and every chapter belongs to a story that never really finishes — because the adventurer keeps logging back in.

What Comes Next

I’m starting fresh. New characters, both games. I won’t tell you the classes yet — not because it’s a secret, but because I genuinely haven’t picked. You’ll know when the first posts land.

The addons are installed. The scripts are running. The Chronicler is waiting, quill poised, mug refilled. In a few days, the first real chapters should start appearing here — not test posts, not demos, but actual stories from actual sessions, written in a voice that treats Azeroth like a place worth writing about.

Because it is.

See you at the inn.

item.title: Picking a main … Forever
item.description: I’ve played a little bit of most of my favorite classes on World of Warcraft Forever, and I’m trying to decide what to main. Somehow it always comes back to Paladin. Personality-wise it just fits me best. I do love mages, mostly for the teleports, because who doesn’t want to skip the boat ride? But I think pally is going to be my thing.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve played a little bit of most of my favorite classes on World of Warcraft Forever, and I’m trying to decide what to main. Somehow it always comes back to Paladin. Personality-wise it just fits me best. I do love mages, mostly for the teleports, because who doesn’t want to skip the boat ride? But I think pally is going to be my thing.

I’m an ex-soldier and a Baha’i, which puts me in a funny spot: I enjoy a good fight, but what I really want is peace and unity. It’s a great contradiction. A Paladin covers both. Hit things with a hammer, then heal everyone afterward.

And let’s not forget the Horde side. My goodness, what a redemption story Forsaken Paladins have! Undead turning back to the Light is better than any 80s comeback montage. I’ll probably play a Forsaken on the PvP phase and a Human for PvE, so I get to see both sides. Once those two hit sixty and are decently geared, I’ll think about leveling that mage. A man can only resist free teleports for so long.

What are y’all planning to play?

item.title: #Welcome to My Azeroth Life
item.content:encoded:
#Welcome to My Azeroth Life

Hi. Hello. Is this thing still on?

This is a reboot of sorts. I used to own this domain and ran a little blog on it. It never went far. Then the domain quietly expired, like a Tamagotchi I forgot to feed. I’m honestly surprised nobody grabbed it while I was gone. Hard to believe the internet didn’t snap it up, but here we are, together again, like a band’s reunion tour nobody asked for.

Then Blizzard announced World of Warcraft: Forever, and it felt like a sign. Everything’s new, and on November 4th everyone starts from zero at the same time. No head starts and no gear gap. It’s just all of us standing in a starting zone, looking at the quest givers and wondering who has the exclamation point. I can’t think of a better time to start over. Full disclosure: I’ve already been poking around in the beta, so I may have a map or two folded in my back pocket.

I’ll probably still wander into retail and other WoW topics now and then. Old habits and all that. Mostly, though, I expect I’ll be living in Forever for a good long while.

So grab a log and pull up a spot by the campfire. Stick around while I ramble about grand adventures in a reborn Azeroth. I promise the stories get better than this one. Probably.

Cheers!
